mean: happening slowly, a little at a time
ex: After his knee surgery, Rohit's recovery was gradual: first a walk to the gate, then to the chai stall.
note: Opposite of sudden. The adverb 'gradually' is very useful: 'Prices gradually came down.'
ex2: There has been a gradual rise in the number of girls playing cricket in small towns.

mean: happening quickly when nobody expects it
ex: A sudden downpour sent the whole Dadar vegetable market running for plastic sheets.
note: The fixed phrase is 'all of a sudden', not 'all of sudden'. Sudden means unexpected; for speed alone, use 'quick' or 'rapid'.
ex2: Dadaji's sudden decision to sell the old family house in Lucknow left everyone stunned.

mean: to get better, or to make something better
ex: Meera wants to improve her spoken English before the campus interviews in Pune.
note: No 'on' for things: 'improve your marks'. 'Improve on' means beat an earlier result: 'improve on last year's score'.
ex2: Ramesh hopes drip irrigation will improve his cotton yield this season.

mean: to become smaller in number or amount, or to make it so
ex: Doctors expect the number of dengue cases to decrease once the monsoon ends.
note: Stress moves: the verb is dee-KREES, the noun is DEE-krees, just like increase. 'A decrease in sales'; 'a decrease of 10%'.
ex2: Our electricity bill should decrease now that the solar panels are up on the roof.

mean: lasting only for a short time, not for ever
ex: Metro work means a temporary diversion near Silk Board for the next two months.
note: Opposite of permanent. Stress the first syllable: TEM-puh-ruh-ree, not tem-po-RA-ry.
ex2: Priya took a temporary job at a Diwali gift shop to save money for her college fees.

mean: to become less or worse; also, to politely say no
ex: Footfall at Kolkata's old single-screen cinemas began to decline once the multiplexes arrived.
note: Also means politely refuse: 'She declined the invitation' is softer than 'refused'. As a noun: 'a decline in sales'.
ex2: Ravi's marks began to decline once he started gaming till two every night.

mean: to change slowly over a long time, usually into something more developed
ex: Film music continues to evolve, mixing Punjabi folk, Carnatic violin and electronic beats.
note: Evolve is slow and natural; for quick or forced change, use 'transform' or 'shift'. Not only animals: ideas, cities and languages evolve.
ex2: Over three generations, the family sweet shop in Varanasi had to evolve to survive, and now it delivers through apps.

mean: firm and steady; not likely to change or fall
ex: After two days in the ICU, the doctor told the family that Nani's condition was finally stable.
note: Indian parents' 'stable job' means a secure one. Noun: stability. A horse's 'stable' is a different word with the same spelling.
ex2: After weeks of wild swings, onion prices at Lasalgaon mandi are finally stable.

mean: very fast; happening in a short time
ex: The rapid spread of UPI means even the sugarcane-juice seller near Charminar now takes payment by QR code.
note: More formal than 'fast'. Use it for change, growth or progress; for a person, say 'a fast runner', not 'a rapid runner'.
ex2: Mumbai's rapid growth means the old chawls of Girgaon are giving way to tall towers.

mean: lasting for ever or for a very long time
ex: After three years on contract, Shalini finally got a permanent post at the district hospital.
note: Indian forms ask for a 'permanent address' (your home town) and a 'present address'. Opposite: temporary.
ex2: The tattoo artist in Goa reminded Karan that the design was permanent and very hard to remove.

mean: old-fashioned; not as good or useful as newer things
ex: The bank's outdated software crashed again, and the queue in Lucknow stretched out of the door.
note: Outdated things are still used but behind the times; obsolete things have mostly stopped being used. An old syllabus is outdated; a typewriter is obsolete.
ex2: Nani's old recipe book has some outdated advice, like adding a big spoon of vanaspati to everything.

mean: to bring back to life, use or strength
ex: Weavers in Chanderi hope that online orders will revive their struggling handloom trade.
note: Used for people (revive a patient), traditions, economies and old songs. Noun: revival.
ex2: A cup of strong filter coffee is enough to revive Lakshmi after a long night shift at the call centre.

mean: to slowly become worse
ex: Delhi's air quality began to deteriorate after Diwali, and schools shifted to online classes.
note: Say all five syllables: dih-TEER-ee-uh-rayt, not 'de-te-rate'. Usually things deteriorate on their own; we rarely say someone deteriorates something.
ex2: Without regular servicing, your scooter's engine will slowly deteriorate.

mean: to stop growing, moving or improving
ex: Without new skills, Farhan feared his career would stagnate in the same back-office job for years.
note: Comes from still, dirty water: a stagnant pond breeds mosquitoes. So it suggests going stale, not just taking a pause.
ex2: Wages in the textile town continued to stagnate even as house rents kept rising.

mean: a sudden, strong rise in amount or number
ex: There is always a surge in train bookings to Patna in the weeks before Chhath Puja.
note: Also a verb: 'The crowd surged forward.' Cab apps use 'surge pricing': fares jump when demand jumps.
ex2: A surge of fans at Gate 3 forced the police to open extra entry counters before the final.

mean: certain to happen; cannot be stopped or avoided
ex: With forty runs needed off two overs and one wicket left, defeat felt inevitable to the Ranchi crowd.
note: Stress the second syllable: in-EV-ih-tuh-bul. 'Accept the inevitable' means stop fighting what must happen.
ex2: With both parents working as doctors, Ishaan's choice of medicine seemed almost inevitable to his relatives.

mean: lasting only a short time; passing quickly
ex: The doctor said Kavya's dizziness was transient and would pass once she drank some ORS.
note: More formal than 'temporary'. A 'transient population' means people who keep moving in and out, like migrant workers or hostel students.
ex2: The counsellor told the Class 12 students that exam stress is usually transient and fades after results.

mean: no longer used because something newer has replaced it
ex: Pagers became obsolete in India almost as soon as cheap mobile phones arrived.
note: Stronger than outdated. 'Render something obsolete' means make it useless: 'Online forms rendered the queue obsolete.'
ex2: Typewriters outside the district court in Lucknow are almost obsolete, though a few old clerks still use them.

mean: never happened or seen before
ex: Chennai received unprecedented rainfall that December, and whole neighbourhoods went under water.
note: News channels overuse it to mean just 'big'. Use it only when something truly has no earlier example.
ex2: The final drew an unprecedented crowd, and fans watched on giant screens across Ahmedabad.

mean: lasting a very long time, or coming back again and again
ex: Waterlogging in Gurugram every monsoon has become a perennial problem.
note: From geography class: a perennial river like the Ganga flows all year, while a seasonal one dries up.
ex2: Lack of parking is a perennial complaint at every meeting of our housing society.

mean: the force or speed that keeps something moving or growing
ex: After two quick boundaries, the momentum shifted and the crowd at Eden Gardens sensed a comeback.
note: It is about keeping going once you have started. In physics, it is mass times velocity.
ex2: The drive to clean the Yamuna ghats gained momentum once college students joined in.

mean: cannot be changed back to how it was
ex: Years of untreated diabetes had caused irreversible damage to Mr Iyer's eyes.
note: Not 'unreversible'. Opposite: reversible.
ex2: Cutting down the old banyan tree would be irreversible, so the panchayat asked for more time to decide.

mean: a state of constant change, where nothing is settled
ex: With the founders leaving and new investors arriving, the startup was in flux for months.
note: Almost always used as 'in flux' or 'in a state of flux'. In everyday speech, 'up in the air' is close.
ex2: Fuel prices were in flux all month, and auto drivers kept changing their fares.

mean: to wear away slowly, little by little
ex: Repeated paper leaks erode students' trust in the exam system.
note: Literally, rivers wear away land, as the Brahmaputra does to Majuli island. Figuratively, inflation erodes savings. Noun: erosion.
ex2: Every monsoon the Brahmaputra continues to erode its banks, and more fields on Majuli island disappear.

mean: lasting a very short time
ex: Rangoli is ephemeral art: hours of careful work, swept away by the next morning.
note: Literary. Use it for striking things that vanish (fame, trends, blossoms). For a short job or fix, plain 'temporary' is better.
ex2: Fame on Instagram is often ephemeral: last month's viral reel is forgotten within a week.

mean: not wanting to change or act; staying the same out of habit
ex: Most people keep the same bank account for decades out of sheer inertia, not loyalty.
note: From physics: things stay still or keep moving unless pushed. In life, it means sticking with what is because change takes effort.
ex2: After the Diwali holidays, Tanvi had to fight her own inertia to get back to the gym.

mean: to become or make bigger in number or amount
ex: Onion prices always increase when heavy rain damages the crop around Nashik.
note: Verb: in-KREES; noun: IN-krees ('a big increase'). Say 'an increase in prices', not 'an increase of prices'.
ex2: The gym trainer told Zoya to increase her weights slowly, a little each week.

mean: happening or made only a short time ago
ex: The recent hike in cooking gas prices has hit every kitchen budget in our colony.
note: 'Recent' is only for the past. For what is coming soon, say 'near future', never 'recent future'.
ex2: Riya's most recent reel, shot at a Jaipur stepwell, got more views than all her others.

mean: happening all the time, or staying the same
ex: The constant honking outside the hospital in Lucknow kept the patients awake all night.
note: Two meanings: 'never stopping' (constant noise) and 'not changing' (a constant speed). 'Constantly' means all the time.
ex2: Coastal Kerala has a fairly constant temperature, so people there barely notice winter.

mean: a change in position, direction or opinion
ex: There has been a big shift in how small-town families shop, from the kirana store to apps.
note: In Indian English 'we shifted to Pune' means moved house; in formal writing say 'moved to'. Use 'a shift in' + noun.
ex2: Commentators noticed a shift in the match after Bumrah's double-wicket over.

mean: to change yourself to suit a new place or situation
ex: It took Tenzing a few months to adapt to the heat when he moved from Sikkim to Chennai.
note: Don't mix up 'adapt' (change to fit) with 'adopt' (take up an idea, or take a child as your own).
ex2: Small shopkeepers had to adapt quickly once customers started paying by QR code.

mean: to keep going up and down
ex: Tomato prices fluctuate wildly: forty rupees a kilo one week, a hundred the next.
note: Used for prices, temperature, moods and numbers. The noun is 'fluctuation'.
ex2: Sanjay's fever continued to fluctuate all night, so his mother checked it every hour.

mean: to slowly become weaker, paler or less clear
ex: Dry the kurtas in the shade, or the bright colours will fade in the Rajasthan sun.
note: 'Fade' is slow. For a sudden loss, use 'vanish' or 'disappear'. 'Fade away' suits sounds, hopes and memories.
ex2: As the train pulled out of Howrah, the beat of the dhak drums began to fade.

mean: to happen faster, or to make something go faster
ex: The new budget aims to accelerate road building in the north-east.
note: Say 'uk-SEL', not 'ak-SEL'. Formal; 'speed up' is fine in casual talk.
ex2: Vikram's coach told him to accelerate in the last two hundred metres of the race.

mean: to slowly become fewer or smaller
ex: As families moved to the cities, the number of children in the village school began to dwindle.
note: Used for numbers, money, supplies or hope. It suggests a sad, steady loss.
ex2: By the last week of the month, Ankit's savings had begun to dwindle to a few hundred rupees.

mean: a complete check and repair, or a big change to a system
ex: The railways announced a complete overhaul of the signal system on the Howrah line.
note: Also a verb: 'overhaul the syllabus'. The noun stresses the first part (OH-vur-hawl); the verb, the last (oh-vur-HAWL).
ex2: Before Diwali, Mummy decided our cluttered kitchen needed an overhaul, not just a quick clean.

mean: to fall suddenly and by a lot
ex: Grape prices can plummet overnight when unseasonal rain hits the vineyards near Nashik.
note: Stronger than 'fall' or 'drop'. Used for prices, temperatures, ratings and numbers.
ex2: Temperatures plummet after sunset in the Thar desert, so carry a shawl to the dunes.

mean: a turning point after which things are very different
ex: The 1991 economic reforms are often called a watershed in India's history.
note: Literally, high ground that divides rivers. News writers love 'a watershed moment'; save it for truly big changes.
ex2: For the girls of Rohtak, Komal's national wrestling gold was a watershed: suddenly every family wanted a wrestler.

mean: likely to change suddenly and without warning
ex: Share prices were volatile all week, and Kunal's small investments rose and fell every day.
note: British say VOL-uh-tile, Americans VOL-uh-tul. Also used for people who anger quickly: 'a volatile temper'.
ex2: The mood at the village meeting turned volatile, so the sarpanch asked everyone to speak in turn.

mean: growing or changing in small steps
ex: The school's results showed incremental gains each year rather than one sudden jump.
note: Common in office and policy talk. Its opposite is 'radical' or 'sweeping' change.
ex2: Shabnam believes in incremental saving: fifty rupees a day in a tin box adds up by Eid.

mean: to become weak because it is not used
ex: After six weeks in a plaster cast, the muscles in Asif's leg began to atrophy.
note: Also a noun: 'muscle atrophy'. Used for bodies, skills and memory, and sometimes for old institutions.
ex2: Musicians say skills atrophy without daily riyaz, so the Ustad's students practise every dawn.

mean: something that belongs to an older time, not the present
ex: In a city of app cabs, Kolkata's yellow Ambassador taxi is a charming anachronism.
note: Two uses: a mistake that puts something in the wrong period (common in films), and a custom that has outlived its time.
ex2: Viewers spotted an anachronism in the 1940s period drama: a plastic water bottle on the table.
